title: Yesterday I… — and verbs that know your gender
title_target: Вчора і завтра — Vchora i zavtra
goal: Say what happened yesterday and what will happen tomorrow, and face something English has no equivalent for: past-tense verbs that change with the speaker's gender.
bekal: form the future tense with буду
tell what happened yesterday in full sentences

dialogs.title: Діалог — Monday morning, a missed class
dialogs.intro: Oksana asks Ani why she wasn't in class. Notice that every past-tense verb Ani uses about herself ends in **-ла**, and every one about Andriy ends in **-в**.

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.literal: Ani, where — you — were (past f) — yesterday?

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: I was at home. I was sick.
lines.literal: I — was (past f) — at-home. I — was-ill (past f).

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: That's a shame! So what did you do?
lines.literal: pity! and — what — you — did (past f)?

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.literal: slept (past f), read (past f), drank (past f) — tea.

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: And Andriy? He wasn't in class either.
lines.literal: and — Andriy? he — also — not — was (past m) — at — class.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: He was working. The café was busy.
lines.literal: he — worked (past m). in — café — was (past n) — many — people (genitive).

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: I see. You both missed the topic.
lines.literal: understandable. you — both — missed (past pl) — topic.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: I know. But I've already read it all at home.
lines.literal: I — know. but — I — already — read-through (past f) — everything — at-home.

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: Well done! Will you be there tomorrow?

lines.speaker: Оксана:
lines.id: Good. Tomorrow we'll talk about the past tense.
lines.literal: good. tomorrow — we — will — talk — about — past — time.

lines.speaker: Ані:
lines.id: Ironic. I've been talking about yesterday all day.
lines.literal: ironic. I — already — whole — day — talk — about — yesterday.

notes: **The past tense doesn't care who is speaking; it cares about gender and number.** Drop **-ти** from the basic form and attach **-в** (m), **-ла** (f), **-ло** (n), or **-ли** (pl). *Читати* → *читав / читала / читало / читали*. It's that simple, and it works for almost every verb.

**If you're a woman, you'll say -ла for the rest of your life.** *Я була*, *я читала*, *я працювала*. If you're a man: *я був*, *я читав*, *я працював*. English has nothing like it, and there's no way around it: every past-tense sentence makes you choose.

**The ending -в sounds like w.** *Був* sounds like *boow*, *читав* like *chi-TAW*, *працював* like *pra-tsyoo-VAW*. This is the most typical Ukrainian sound, and getting it right instantly sets you apart from someone reading off a page.

**Було is used for sentences with no subject.** *У кафе було багато людей*: literally "in the café there was many people". Sentences like this use the neuter form because there is no subject with a gender. Likewise: *Було холодно* (it was cold), *Було цікаво* (it was interesting).

**Some verbs change their stem in the past tense.** *Йти* → *йшов / йшла / йшли*. *Могти* → *міг / могла / могли*. *Їсти* → *їв / їла / їли*. There are only a few, and they're all common verbs, so they'll stick through repetition, not memorization.

**Прочитала is more than читала.** The prefix **про-** marks the action as finished: *читала* (was reading, did some reading), *прочитала* (read it all the way through). Pairs like this are called aspect, and that's A2 material. For now, just know that a prefix often means "done".

**The Ukrainian future has two routes, and the second doesn't exist in Russian.** *Буду читати* (compound) and *читатиму* (one word) mean the same. The one-word form sounds more natural to Ukrainian ears, and using it now and then instantly shows that you learned Ukrainian.

grammars.title: The past tense: one ending, four choices
after: The last three rows are irregular and must be memorized. Luckily they're verbs you'll say dozens of times a week, so they'll stick on their own.

grammars.title: The future: two equal routes
body: Use either one; both are correct and both are common.
after: Look at the middle row of the second table: in the present tense the verb **disappears entirely**. This goes back to Unit 1: only the present tense can do without a verb.

blocks.text: Notice that past time expressions use родовий (genitive): *минулого тижня*, *минулого року*. It's the same pattern as dates, and you'll meet it again when you give your birthday.

blocks.title: Four past-tense sentences you'll use all the time
items: **Я був / була…** — I was (in)… *Я була в Києві.*
**Мені сподобалося** — I liked it (something already over). The standard sentence after a film, a meal, or a trip.
**Я не знав / не знала** — I didn't know. A lifesaver in a hundred situations.
**Що ти робив / робила вчора?** — what did you do yesterday? The most common conversation opener.
⚠️ Notice that all four make you choose a gender. Practice the form that applies to you until it comes out without thinking.

blocks.text: When you need time to think

This isn't grammar, but it saves more conversations than any grammar: **Хвилинку** (just a moment), **Як це сказати...** (how do I put it), **Я подумаю** (let me think). Ukrainians use them too, and using them makes you sound like someone thinking in Ukrainian, not someone translating.
